### Why hardwood treads hold up better on stairs than resilient flooring
Stairs take a different kind of wear than open floor - every step is a point-load impact right at the nose, where your foot lands hardest going down. Florida Residential Code R311.7.5 sets stair nosing at 3/4 in. to 1-1/4 in. on stairs with solid risers, and hardwood treads are milled to that dimension as one solid piece, not a separate strip glued to the tread's leading edge. That's the structural reason a hardwood or engineered tread tends to outlast a vinyl-clad one on the same staircase. Sand also finds its way onto stairs faster than a straight-line hallway does, especially in a barrier-island or beach-adjacent home where shoes come off at the door but sandy feet still climb to the second floor. That grit acts like sandpaper on a glued vinyl seam at the tread edge, which is one more reason the nosing on a resilient stair tread tends to fail before the rest of the plank does.

### Cost: vinyl treads vs hardwood treads
Tread option Cost per tread, installed (2026) LVP tread, fully glued $65-$105 Laminate tread $55-$85 Engineered hardwood tread $110-$180 Solid hardwood tread $130-$220 Vinyl treads cost less per step up front, but factor in that a nosing failure means redoing that step within a few years. For a lot of Sarasota and Manatee County homeowners doing an LVP whole-house job, paying the difference for hardwood treads once - rather than a vinyl tread that may need reworking - is the calculation that tips the decision. See our full stair treads cost guide for how these numbers scale across a whole flight, or start with a free estimate to get both options priced side by side.

## Can you put vinyl plank flooring on a lanai or in a Florida room with no AC?
URL: https://sarasotaflooringcompany.com/blog/put-vinyl-plank-flooring-lanai-florida-room-no/

In a Sarasota-area lanai or Florida room with no AC, yes — if you choose the right core and float it rather than glue it: COREtec approves those spaces only for floating installs, rating SPC for -25°F to 155°F versus just 32°F to 100°F for WPC. Direct sun still matters separately, so an unshaded lanai needs film or blinds even with the right core.

### Can You Put Vinyl Plank Flooring on a Lanai or Florida Room With No AC?
You can, with two conditions. First, the room has to be what COREtec's installation guide calls a three-season space, meaning it's enclosed but not climate-controlled, and its published spec only approves that use case for a floating install, never glue-down. Second, the core matters: COREtec rates its SPC lines for -25°F to 155°F after installation, but its WPC lines are only rated 32°F to 100°F, and a closed-up lanai in August can push past that WPC ceiling on a bad afternoon. We cover the core choice itself in more depth in our post on SPC vs WPC for Florida heat . This comes up constantly in this market, since a huge share of Sarasota and Manatee County homes have a lanai or converted Florida room that was never wired into the main AC system, and homeowners often don't realize the flooring spec changes once a room falls outside climate control. We ask directly at the estimate whether a mini-split or window unit runs in that room full time, occasionally, or not at all, since that single answer changes both the core and install method we'll recommend, and it's a different answer for nearly every property we visit, even within the same neighborhood.

### Why Floating Installs Are the Only Option There
A glue-down floor bonds the plank rigidly to the substrate, so when temperature swings cause the plank to expand and contract, that stress has nowhere to go and the bond itself can fail over time. A floating floor rides on top of an underlayment and isn't locked to the slab, so it can expand and contract as a connected sheet within the expansion gap left at the walls. That's exactly why manufacturers restrict uncooled, three-season spaces to floating installs only; it isn't a suggestion, it's the condition attached to the warranty. We size that expansion gap a bit more generously than usual in these rooms too, since the temperature range they experience over a full year is wider than a climate-controlled interior room ever sees.

### What About Direct Sun on the Lanai?
Temperature rating and sun exposure are two separate problems. COREtec's own guide also warns against prolonged direct sunlight regardless of core type, recommending drapes, blinds, or in a lanai's case, exterior shading or window film during peak hours to limit discoloration and thermal expansion. If your lanai gets hit with sun most of the day and has no meaningful shade, porcelain tile is worth considering instead. Under TCNA's EJ171 guidance, tile in direct sunlight or exposed to moisture needs movement joints every 8-12 feet, tighter than the 20-25 foot spacing used indoors, which is the tile world's version of the same expansion problem vinyl faces.

### Our Approach for These Rooms
We ask about AC access and sun exposure before we ever recommend a product for a lanai or Florida room, because the right answer changes room to room even on the same property. Floating SPC with a proper expansion gap is our usual starting point; if the space gets hammered by afternoon sun with no shade options, we'll walk you through tile instead. Run your room through our Florida flooring finder tool to see which materials fit your specific setup, and check our vinyl plank flooring cost guide for what a floating SPC install in a lanai typically runs. Bring us a few photos of the room and its sun exposure through the day if you can, since that alone often narrows the material list before we even schedule the visit.

## How much does porcelain tile installation cost per square foot?
URL: https://sarasotaflooringcompany.com/blog/porcelain-tile-installation-cost-per-square-foot/

Installed porcelain or ceramic tile typically runs $6 to $15 per square foot in Sarasota and Manatee County in 2026. Standard 12-18 in. tile costs $6-$10, large-format 24 in.-plus tile costs $9-$15, and wood-look plank tile costs $8-$13. Large-format tile costs more because it demands a flatter substrate and more precise layout to avoid lippage.

### What Does Porcelain Tile Cost Per Square Foot Installed?
Standard 12-18 in. porcelain or ceramic tile runs $6-$10 per square foot installed. Large-format tile, 24 in. and up, runs $9-$15, and wood-look plank tile, the long narrow format made to mimic hardwood, runs $8-$13. HomeGuide's 2026 national data reports a wider band, $15-$50 per square foot installed with labor alone at $12-$30, which reflects markets and tile grades well above the standard product most Sarasota homeowners choose. Our ranges are what we actually quote on Gulf Coast jobs, for tile contractors who show up, measure and price the actual room rather than a national average. Natural stone runs higher, $12-$22 per square foot, because it's heavier, more porous and needs sealing that porcelain doesn't. Travertine and marble also need a more careful substrate check before installation, since both crack more readily than porcelain over a subfloor that flexes even slightly.

### Why Large-Format Tile Costs More to Install
Tile size drives labor more than it drives material cost. ANSI A108.02, the industry installation standard, requires that for any tile with an edge 15 in. or longer the substrate can vary no more than 1/8 in. over 10 ft and 1/16 in. over 24 in. A standard 12 in. tile can hide a little waviness in an old slab; a 24 in. or 30 in. plank can't, so it shows lippage at the edges if the floor underneath isn't flat enough. That means large-format jobs more often need self-leveling underlayment before tile goes down, which runs $250-$700 per room and is a separate line item, not folded into the tile price. It's also why large-format layouts take longer to dry-fit and cut around vents, thresholds and outlets, which shows up as more labor hours on the quote. Trowel notch size and thinset coverage also change with tile size; a 24 in. plank needs a larger-format trowel and closer to full mortar coverage on the back of the tile to avoid hollow spots, which a smaller 12 in. tile is more forgiving about.

### Showers and Backsplash Pricing
Bathroom work prices by the project rather than by the square foot, because a shower involves waterproofing and slope, not just tile. A Kerdi waterproofed shower runs $1,800-$3,800, and a curbless shower with a linear drain, the barrier-free style common in universal-design remodels, runs $2,800-$5,200. Kitchen and bath backsplash tile, a smaller area with more cutting around outlets and cabinets, runs $22-$45 per square foot. Shower pricing is a project total rather than a per-square-foot rate because most of the labor is in the waterproofing membrane and the slope to the drain, not the tile itself. A small shower with intricate niche work can cost more per square foot than a much larger, simpler wall.

### Getting a Real Number for Your Floor
Tile pricing depends on tile size, substrate condition and whether old flooring has to come out first, so a square-footage number alone won't tell you much. We check the subfloor and, on a slab, take a moisture reading before quoting, then write a line-itemized estimate that separates material, labor, prep and removal. We quote tile jobs the same way for a condo on Siesta Key as for a single-family home inland, adjusting for whatever the subfloor actually needs. See tile options on our tile installation page, or check full pricing on the tile cost guide . If you're replacing old tile, our tile removal page covers demo separately. Request a free estimate to get exact numbers for your room.

## Do I need a permit to replace flooring in Sarasota County?
URL: https://sarasotaflooringcompany.com/blog/permit-replace-flooring-sarasota-county/

Sarasota County generally treats flooring replacement, tile, vinyl plank, hardwood or laminate, as cosmetic work that doesn't require a building permit, as long as there's no change to the subfloor structure or layout. Condo buildings are the exception: HOA rules on sound underlayment can still apply even when the county doesn't require a permit. Confirm specifics with the county building department for your address.

### Do You Need a Permit to Replace Flooring in Sarasota County?
For most homes, no. Swapping carpet, tile, laminate or vinyl for new flooring is considered cosmetic work in Sarasota County when it doesn't touch the subfloor structure, and cosmetic work generally doesn't trigger a building permit. Homeowners are often surprised how broad that cosmetic category is; it covers the overwhelming majority of flooring jobs we do across Sarasota, Manatee and Charlotte counties, whether it's a whole-house vinyl plank install or a single bathroom retiled with tile . That's consistent with how most Florida counties handle finish flooring generally: it's treated like painting or changing countertops, a cosmetic update rather than construction that touches the building's structure, electrical or plumbing systems.

### When Flooring Work Could Need a Permit
The line moves once the job touches structure. Removing and replacing a plywood subfloor, changing a slab's elevation, or altering load paths near a wall are structural changes, and those typically do need a permit regardless of what finish flooring goes on top. If your project includes moving walls, changing a staircase's structure, or major subfloor repair rather than straightforward flooring replacement, that's a different conversation than a standard install, and one worth having with the building department directly rather than assuming either way. Self-leveling underlayment to correct a low spot in a slab, on its own, usually stays on the cosmetic side of that line, since it's a topping applied over the existing slab rather than a structural change to it. It's worth mentioning during your estimate anyway, since it changes the scope and timeline of the job even when it doesn't change the permit picture.

### Condos Play by Different Rules
County permitting and HOA approval aren't the same thing. Even when the county doesn't require a permit for a cosmetic flooring swap, your condo association can still require review and approval, particularly for hard-surface flooring on upper floors where sound transmission between units matters. That's a building-specific requirement layered on top of, not instead of, county rules. This comes up constantly in barrier-island buildings around Siesta Key , where older buildings with concrete floor-ceiling assemblies weren't designed with today's underlayment standards in mind, so boards lean on their own approval process to manage sound complaints between neighbors.

### How to Confirm Before You Start
Rules can vary slightly by jurisdiction within our service area and by the specific scope of work, so we recommend a quick call to the Sarasota County Building Department for your specific address if you're unsure, especially on anything beyond a straightforward flooring swap. We'll also flag it during your free estimate if we see anything that looks like it crosses into structural or subfloor work beyond a normal flooring swap. A permit question is one of the few things worth confirming before demo starts rather than during it. Once old flooring is out and a crew is standing in your living room, that's a bad moment to discover the scope needs a permit filing that adds days to the timeline. A short phone call before the estimate, or a question raised during it, avoids that entirely, and it costs nothing but a few minutes to ask before crews and material are already committed and scheduled to show up at your address. If you're in a condo, see our condo flooring page and the condo flooring approval checklist tool before you order material. Request a free estimate and we'll walk through what your specific project needs.

## Do I need a permit to change the flooring in a Florida condo?
URL: https://sarasotaflooringcompany.com/blog/permit-change-flooring-florida-condo/

It depends on your city and your association. Several Florida cities, including Miami, Miami Beach, Boca Raton and Tampa, require a building permit plus an acoustic affidavit for hard-surface flooring in condos. Regardless of local permit rules, the Florida Building Code requires floor-ceiling assemblies between dwelling units to meet IIC and STC ratings of 50, or 45 if field-tested, which is what most HOA flooring rules are built around.

### Does Your Florida Condo Flooring Change Need a Permit?
There's no single statewide answer, because condo flooring permitting is set city by city, not by the state. Some Florida cities, Miami, Miami Beach, Boca Raton and Tampa among them, require a building permit and an acoustic affidavit before hard-surface flooring goes in over an occupied unit below. Practice in Sarasota, Manatee and Charlotte county buildings varies more by individual association than by city ordinance, so the HOA is usually the first call, not the building department. That's a meaningful difference from a single-family home, where we can usually tell you within the first few minutes of a free estimate whether county permitting applies at all. Condo buildings add a second layer, the association's own architectural review process, that a county permit search won't show you, and that layer is often the slower of the two to clear, since a volunteer board typically meets on its own monthly schedule rather than a permit office's posted turnaround time.

### The Sound Rating Every Condo Rule Is Built Around
Whether or not a permit is required, the underlying standard is consistent: the Florida Building Code requires floor-ceiling assemblies between dwelling units to meet an Impact Insulation Class (IIC) and Sound Transmission Class (STC) of 50, or 45 if measured with field testing rather than lab testing. That's the number most HOA flooring committees are checking for when they ask for an underlayment spec sheet, even if they don't cite the code section by name. Vinyl plank and tile installed directly over a slab, with no acoustic underlayment, essentially never meets that rating in an older building, because impact sound from footsteps transmits straight through the concrete to the unit below. That's the whole reason acoustic underlayment exists as a product category, and it's why HOA-approved flooring lists almost always name a specific underlayment product alongside the finish material.

### Who Can Pull the Permit in a Multi-Family Building
When a permit is required, it's often not something a condo owner can pull as an owner-builder the way they might for a single-family house. In Longboat Key, for example, the town's building department FAQ notes that owners cannot pull owner-builder permits in multi-family buildings; a licensed contractor has to file for the permit. If your building requires a permit, plan on the contractor handling that filing rather than doing it yourself. That's a practical reason to loop your contractor in early, before you've ordered material, rather than after. A contractor who's used to condo work in your building or a similar one nearby can usually tell you upfront whether the city and the association are going to want a permit, an affidavit, or both, which saves a round trip to the board after material is already sitting in a storage unit somewhere in the building.

### What to Check Before You Order Flooring
Start with your HOA or condo board's flooring policy, then confirm whether your city requires a permit or affidavit on top of that. Upper-floor units in Siesta Key and Longboat Key buildings especially tend to have specific underlayment requirements tied to the IIC/STC 50 standard. Our condo flooring approval checklist tool walks through what boards typically ask for, and our condo flooring page covers underlayment options that meet the code minimum. For the board approval process itself, see our guide on getting HOA approval for new flooring . Request a free estimate and we'll help you gather what your board or building department needs before material gets ordered.

## Does new flooring increase home value?
URL: https://sarasotaflooringcompany.com/blog/new-flooring-increase-home-value/

Yes, and refinishing pays back more than replacing. The 2022 National Association of Realtors/NARI Remodeling Impact Report found hardwood floor refinishing recovered 147% of its cost at resale, while installing new wood flooring recovered 118%. A typical $3,400 refinish added about $5,000 in perceived value, according to the same report.

### Does New Flooring Increase Home Value?
According to the National Association of Realtors' 2022 Remodeling Impact Report, produced with NARI, hardwood floor refinishing recovered 147% of its cost at resale, and installing new wood flooring recovered 118%. Both numbers are well above what most remodeling categories recover at resale, where cost recovery well under 100% is the norm rather than the exception. Flooring, and refinishing specifically, is one of the higher-return interior projects tracked anywhere in that report. That puts flooring in the same conversation as kitchen and bath updates, which typically top most ROI lists, rather than the lower-return category where a lot of purely cosmetic projects, fresh paint aside, tend to land once you account for material and labor.

### Refinishing vs. New Flooring: Which Pays Back More
The report put a typical hardwood refinish at $3,400, adding roughly $5,000 in perceived value at resale, a return that new flooring installation doesn't quite match dollar for dollar even though it still recovers most of its cost. That makes sense structurally: refinishing an existing hardwood floor that's in good condition is cheaper labor and no material cost at all, while new flooring installation carries full material and labor costs from the start, even though buyers respond well to both outcomes at showing time. Neither number means every floor in your house is worth touching before a sale. A refinish only pays off on a floor that's structurally sound under the wear; a floor with cupping, deep gouges or water damage usually needs replacement regardless of which line item looks better on paper, since sanding can't fix a board that's already structurally compromised, no matter how good the finish coat looks in the days right after the crew leaves. See our guide on whether to replace floors before selling for that decision specifically.

### Why We're Citing a 2022 Report
The 2022 NAR/NARI Remodeling Impact Report is the most recent edition that tracked flooring specifically; the 2025 edition doesn't include a flooring category. We'd rather point to the last solid data than make up a newer number, so treat these figures as directionally reliable rather than current-year statistics. Materials, labor rates and buyer expectations have all shifted since 2022, but the underlying pattern, that flooring in good repair sells a house more easily than flooring that reads as a problem to a walkthrough buyer, hasn't changed just because the survey wasn't repeated in a later year.

### What This Means If You're Selling in Sarasota
If your existing hardwood is in decent shape under the wear, refinishing is worth pricing out before you jump to full replacement, since the data suggests it returns more per dollar spent. If the floor is beyond refinishing, or you're dealing with worn carpet or dated tile, new flooring still recovers most of its cost and tends to be one of the changes buyers notice first when they walk in. A pre-listing walkthrough with an installer, not just your agent, can settle the refinish-versus-replace question with a real number rather than a guess, and it typically takes less than an hour of your time to get one, which is usually the deciding factor between the two options once the numbers are actually in front of you. See what Florida buyers specifically respond to on our post about what flooring Florida home buyers want , or get a read on refinish vs. replace for your floor with a free estimate . Refinishing options are on our hardwood floor refinishing page.

## Can mold grow under vinyl plank flooring on a Florida slab?
URL: https://sarasotaflooringcompany.com/blog/mold-grow-under-vinyl-plank-flooring-florida-slab/

Yes -- mold can grow under vinyl plank on a Florida slab when the concrete emits moisture above the flooring's rated limit, commonly 75% to 85% relative humidity. Floating installation doesn't remove this risk, it just changes how the failure shows up. The EPA says materials should dry within 24-48 hours after any water event to keep mold from establishing.

### Yes, and Here's the Mechanism
Yes, mold can grow under vinyl plank flooring on a Florida slab, and it doesn't need standing water to do it. A concrete slab is porous. Moisture from the ground below, or from a slab that simply hasn't finished curing and off-gassing water, moves up through it constantly, a process called moisture vapor emission. Vinyl plank, especially fully adhered glue-down waterproof flooring , traps that moisture between the slab and the plank instead of letting it evaporate into the room the way an uncovered floor would. Organic residue in adhesive, dust trapped during installation, and the warm, dark, enclosed space under the plank give mold everything it needs except the moisture itself, and a slab running above its rated limit supplies exactly that.

### Floating Doesn't Remove the Moisture Limit, It Just Moves Where It Fails
A common assumption is that floating vinyl plank, the kind that clicks together without glue, sidesteps this problem because there's no adhesive bond to fail. It doesn't. Most manufacturers of floating LVP and LVT still cap acceptable in-slab relative humidity at 75% to 85%, the same order of magnitude as a glue-down install. What changes is which failure shows up first: a glued floor tends to show adhesive bond loss and lifting, while a floating floor over a too-wet slab tends to show dimensional problems, planks that won't stay locked, edges that swell, and underneath, the same warm, damp, low-airflow conditions that let mold and mildew take hold.

### The 24-to-48-Hour Window That Matters Most
The EPA's guidance on mold and moisture is blunt about timing: dry any water-damaged material within 24 to 48 hours, or mold can start to establish itself. That window applies just as much to a slab that got wet from a leak, an AC condensate line, or storm intrusion before vinyl plank ever goes down, and it applies just as much to floors that are already installed. If a room floods, or a slab sits wet under old flooring that's being removed, the clock on mold risk is already running before a new floor is even ordered, which is one more reason a moisture test comes before, not after, a vinyl plank quote gets written.

### What We Test Before Vinyl Plank Goes Down
We test relative humidity in the slab with a probe set at 40% of the slab's depth, the standard depth for a slab drying from one side, before quoting vinyl plank flooring over concrete anywhere in our service area. A reading above roughly 75% RH under the ASTM F710/F2170 default limit means we're talking about a vapor-retarder system, a different product line rated for higher moisture, or slab drying time before installation, not proceeding as planned. Our guide on moisture barriers for vinyl plank over concrete covers what actually stops this at the source.

### What It Looks and Smells Like Before You See Mold
Most homeowners notice the smell before they see anything: a musty odor that's strongest right after the AC kicks on, especially near an exterior wall or a spot that's flooded before. Discoloration along the seams, planks that feel slightly soft or spongy underfoot, or a floor that seems to sweat on humid mornings are all worth a look before they turn into a bigger problem. None of that is a diagnosis you can make by smell alone, though; pulling a plank and testing what's underneath is the only way to know whether it's condensation, a slab still curing, or an actual moisture failure. If you're already seeing visible mold, a repair assessment is the place to start rather than replacing the whole room blind.

## Do I need a moisture barrier under vinyl plank flooring on a concrete slab?
URL: https://sarasotaflooringcompany.com/blog/moisture-barrier-under-vinyl-plank-flooring-concrete-slab/

It depends on the product, but often yes. Most floating LVP and LVT makers cap acceptable in-slab relative humidity at 75% to 85%; some rigid SPC lines allow up to 90% RH or 8 lbs per 1,000 sq ft per 24 hours within the manufacturer's tested system. A slab above the rated limit needs a vapor-retarder layer before vinyl plank goes down in a Sarasota-area home.

### The Short Answer: It Depends on the Product, Not Just the Slab
Whether you need a separate moisture barrier under vinyl plank on a concrete slab depends on which product you're installing, because manufacturers set their own limits and their own required assemblies. Most floating LVP and LVT lines still cap acceptable in-slab relative humidity at 75% to 85%; go above that and the manufacturer's warranty typically requires a rated vapor-retarder layer between the slab and the plank, not just a slightly thicker foam pad underneath. Some rigid SPC lines allow more: Shaw's Floorte Pro guide permits up to 8 lbs per 1,000 sq ft per 24 hours (ASTM F1869) or 90% relative humidity (ASTM F2170) in its tested system, with slab pH capped at 9 to 10 and three moisture tests required for the first 1,000 sq ft of any given room or open floor plan.

### Why Floating Doesn't Get You Off the Hook
A floating floor, the kind that clicks together without glue, feels like it should sidestep slab moisture entirely since nothing is bonded to the concrete. It doesn't remove the limit, it just changes what fails when the slab is too wet. Instead of adhesive bond loss, a floating floor over an unaddressed wet slab tends to show swelling at the plank edges, locking mechanisms that won't stay tight, and the damp, low-airflow conditions underneath that support mold. The manufacturer's moisture cap still applies whether the floor is glued or floating; it's written into the warranty either way.

### What Actually Counts as a Barrier
A moisture barrier isn't the thin foam pad that comes attached to some click-together vinyl planks; that pad manages sound and comfort, not vapor. Mohawk's laminate installation guidance, which applies the same underlying principle to floating floors over concrete, calls for 6-mil polyethylene sheeting with seams overlapped at least 8 in., taped and run up the walls behind the baseboard. For vinyl plank specifically, that can mean a rated underlayment with a built-in vapor layer, a liquid-applied membrane troweled onto the slab, or, on the glue-down side, a moisture-mitigating adhesive rated for the reading you actually measured. Slab leveling and moisture prep is where this usually gets addressed before flooring is ordered.

### What This Means for Your Quote
We test the slab before writing a vinyl plank flooring quote, not after, because the test result changes the line items on the quote itself. A clean reading under a product's stated limit needs no extra barrier beyond the standard underlayment. A high reading adds a vapor-retarder line, sometimes a different product line rated for wetter slabs, and occasionally a slab-drying delay before install. Here's exactly how we run that test , and what the numbers mean once we have them.

### How This Compares to Laminate Over the Same Slab
Laminate flooring uses similar logic but a more specific spec: Mohawk's laminate guidance calls for 6-mil polyethylene film under every floating laminate installation over concrete, full stop, with no moisture-percentage exception built in the way some SPC vinyl lines allow. That makes laminate a slightly less forgiving product on a borderline slab reading, since the barrier isn't optional above some threshold, it's simply required regardless of how the slab tests. If you're weighing laminate against vinyl plank for the same room, our laminate-specific moisture barrier guide walks through that requirement in more detail, including how it interacts with the 8 in. seam overlap the film needs at every joint, and why we still test the slab before ordering either product for a Bradenton or Sarasota home.

## Do you need a moisture barrier under laminate on a concrete floor?
URL: https://sarasotaflooringcompany.com/blog/moisture-barrier-under-laminate-concrete-floor/

Yes, in a Sarasota-area home on a slab. Mohawk's laminate installation guide requires a moisture barrier over any concrete floor — 6-mil polyethylene film with seams overlapped 8 inches for a floating install. The slab should also test within ASTM F1869's default limit of 3 lbs of moisture vapor emission per 1,000 sq ft per 24 hours, unless the manufacturer allows a higher reading.

### Do You Need a Moisture Barrier Under Laminate on a Concrete Floor?
Yes, and it's not optional if you want the warranty to hold. Mohawk's laminate installation FAQ specifies a moisture barrier over concrete for every floating laminate install: 6-mil polyethylene film, with seams overlapped 8 inches and taped, running up the wall slightly behind the baseboard, with every seam taped rather than just overlapped loosely. That film blocks vapor moving up through the slab from ever reaching the laminate's wood-fiber core, which is the part of the floor most vulnerable to swelling and delamination once moisture gets to it. This applies whether the slab is brand new or decades old. A newer pour can actually test wetter for longer than an older one, since concrete keeps releasing residual moisture from the curing process for months, sometimes longer than a year on a thick slab. That's a common surprise on new-construction homes in Lakewood Ranch and Parrish, where owners assume a brand-new slab must be the driest option in the house and are caught off guard when the moisture test says otherwise.

### How Much Moisture Is Too Much?
A barrier alone doesn't fix a slab that's too wet to begin with. The standard test, ASTM F1869, uses a calcium chloride kit taped to the slab for 60-72 hours to measure moisture vapor emission rate. The default acceptable limit is 3 lbs per 1,000 sq ft per 24 hours, unless the specific laminate manufacturer's documentation allows a higher number for their product. A slab that fails that test needs a sealer or a longer drying period before laminate goes down, barrier or not. We schedule this test well ahead of the install date specifically because the 60-72 hour window doesn't fit into a same-week timeline if the first reading comes back high and a second test is needed after treatment.

### What Happens If You Skip the Barrier?
We've torn out laminate installed without one, and the failure pattern is consistent: swelling and lifting starting at the seams, usually noticeable within the first year, worse in rooms that stay humid longer between AC cycles, like a back bedroom on a thermostat zone that runs less often than the main living space. It's an expensive way to find out a step got skipped, since the whole floating floor typically has to come up rather than just the affected boards. A 6-mil film and a moisture test add a modest amount to the job cost and prevent nearly all of that risk. We include both as standard line items on every laminate quote rather than treating them as optional upgrades, since the cost of doing it right the first time is small next to tearing out an entire floating floor a year later.

### How We Handle Barrier and Moisture Testing
We test every slab before ordering laminate material and install the polyethylene barrier as a standard part of the job, never as an optional upsell tacked on later. If your slab tests high, we'll walk through the available options with you, from a longer dry-out period to switching to a product built for wetter conditions, such as waterproof vinyl plank . See our laminate flooring cost guide for what barrier and prep typically add to a project, or our subfloor leveling page if the slab needs more than moisture control before installation. Every reading we take gets written into your quote, so there's a clear record of what the slab tested at on the day the barrier went down.

## LVP vs porcelain tile: which is better for a Florida house?
URL: https://sarasotaflooringcompany.com/blog/lvp-vs-porcelain-tile-better-florida-house/

For most Sarasota-area homes, LVP installs faster and costs less than porcelain tile — a two-person crew can lay about 1,000 square feet of click LVP in 1-2 days on a flat, prepped slab, while tile takes longer because of cure times. Our verdict: choose LVP for speed and warmth underfoot, porcelain for wet areas and long-term durability.

### Which Is Better for a Florida House, LVP or Porcelain Tile?
Both materials are effectively waterproof, so the decision usually comes down to timeline, budget and how the room gets used. A two-person crew can install roughly 1,000 sq ft of click-together LVP in one to two days on a flat, prepped slab. Porcelain tile takes several times longer, because thinset and grout need cure time between steps, and that adds up fast if you're re-flooring a whole house instead of one bathroom. Cost tracks the same pattern. This Old House puts national installed LVP costs at roughly $5-$20 per sq ft depending on product grade, while porcelain typically runs higher once labor for cutting and setting is factored in. For a house you're not planning to leave for months, that install-time gap is often the deciding factor as much as price. We saw this play out on a 1,800 sq ft single-story home off Bee Ridge Road last season: the owners had budgeted for tile throughout, then switched the bedrooms and hallway to LVP once they realized the whole project would run nearly two weeks longer with tile in every room instead of four days.

### Cost and Install Time Side by Side
LVP / SPC Porcelain tile Typical installed cost (2026) $1.75–$9.50/sq ft $6–$15/sq ft Install pace, 1,000 sq ft 1-2 days, flat prepped slab Several days to a week or more, cure time between steps Feels like Warmer underfoot, some flex Cold, hard, very stable Best for Living areas, bedrooms, whole-house speed Showers, kitchens, high-traffic wet zones Sources: Sarasota Flooring Company price list (2026); This Old House vinyl plank cost guide. The install-pace gap widens even more on a two-story job, since tile setters generally can't stack loaded thinset trowels and grout buckets on stairs the way an LVP crew can carry pre-cut planks up in bundles.

### Where Porcelain Pulls Ahead
Porcelain wins on raw durability and water performance. To legally carry the name, a tile has to absorb 0.5% water or less under ANSI A137.1, tested to ASTM C373 — that's a lab standard, not a sales pitch, and it's why a shower pan or a Siesta Key lanai transition holds up to standing water better under tile than under almost anything else. Porcelain also doesn't scratch the way vinyl can under grit or furniture legs, which matters in an entryway that sees beach traffic all summer. The tradeoff is comfort and noise. Tile is cold underfoot in January and loud with hard-sole shoes or a dog's nails, and grout lines need periodic sealing, typically every one to two years, to stay stain-resistant. Large-format porcelain reduces the grout-line count and softens that noise issue somewhat, though it also demands a flatter slab to install correctly.

### Where LVP Pulls Ahead
LVP wins on speed, upfront cost and comfort. It installs faster, flexes slightly so it's easier on your feet and back over a long day, and a scratched or damaged plank can be replaced individually instead of chiseling out thinset. The one real weak spot is sun: COREtec's own installation guide warns against prolonged direct sunlight on vinyl planks and recommends drapes or blinds during peak hours, because heat buildup can cause discoloration and thermal expansion at a west-facing sliding door. Plenty of our clients don't pick one exclusively. A common approach in this market is porcelain in the kitchen, entry and bathrooms, with LVP running through bedrooms and living areas, which keeps the highest-wear, wettest rooms on the more durable material without paying tile pricing across the whole square footage. Not sure which split fits your specific rooms and budget? Run your square footage through our Florida flooring finder tool , and see our waterproof flooring guide for how the two materials handle a flood event differently.

## Is LVP or tile the smarter choice for a long-term rental property?
URL: https://sarasotaflooringcompany.com/blog/lvp-tile-smarter-choice-long-term-rental-property/

For a long-term Florida rental, 20-mil rigid-core LVP typically installs for $2.75-$5.50 per square foot versus roughly $6-$10 for 12-18 inch porcelain tile, per local 2026 ranges. LVP is cheaper and faster to replace between tenants; tile lasts longer under heavy traffic but costs more up front and takes longer to redo.

### Cost Per Square Foot: What Landlords Actually Pay
Our typical 2026 local ranges put mid-range 20-mil SPC LVP at $2.75-$5.50 per square foot installed, against $6-$10 per square foot for 12-18 inch porcelain tile . That gap adds up fast across a multi-unit property, which is why LVP tends to be the default for landlords managing several units on a budget. Material cost is only part of the picture for a landlord running several units. Ordering the same LVP product across multiple properties also simplifies inventory, if a plank gets damaged in unit 3, the same box of spare material works for unit 7, which isn't true if every unit has a different tile pattern. We can usually source the same LVP line consistently for a year or two before a manufacturer changes a run, which matters if you're trying to keep flooring consistent across a growing portfolio.

### Wear and Tear: What Holds Up Between Tenants
Tile's durability is rated on the PEI scale, which runs 0 to 5: PEI 2 suits light traffic like bathrooms and bedrooms, PEI 3 covers all residential floors, and PEI 4 handles heavy residential to medium commercial use, the range most rental common areas fall into. For LVP, wear-layer thickness plays a similar role; a 20-mil wear layer is the usual commercial-grade minimum, recommended over the standard 12-mil for rentals with regular tenant turnover. Pets are the wildcard in this comparison. A dog's claws can scratch even a 20-mil wear layer over years of daily use, while tile's hard surface resists scratching almost entirely, though a dropped bowl or a slid piece of furniture can chip it. Neither material is scratch-proof; they just fail differently. If scratching is your main concern, ask about a matte or textured LVP finish, which hides light surface wear better than a high-gloss finish does.

### Turnaround Speed Between Leases
A two-person crew can lay about 1,000 square feet of click LVP in one to two days on a ready slab, while tile needs 24 hours before grouting and up to 72 hours before heavy loads return. If speed between leases matters more than upfront durability, that gap favors LVP; we cover both timelines in more depth in separate posts on fast turnarounds and whole-house timelines . Vacancy carries a real cost for a landlord; every extra day a unit sits empty for flooring work is a day without rent coming in. That's the practical reason speed matters here beyond simple convenience, and it's a bigger factor for a single-unit landlord than for one managing a large portfolio with staggered lease dates.

### Which We'd Recommend, and When
For turnover-heavy properties where cost and speed matter most, we typically lean toward 20-mil LVP. For common areas or units with pets prone to scratching floors, tile's higher PEI rating holds up longer despite the higher upfront cost and slower redo time. There isn't a single right answer across an entire portfolio; it depends on how often you're actually replacing the floor. A mixed approach works too: LVP throughout the bedrooms and living areas, with tile reserved for kitchens, bathrooms, and entryways where water exposure and heavy foot traffic overlap. That split keeps replacement costs down in the rooms that turn over most often while putting the more durable material where it earns its keep. Bring your unit mix, bedrooms, wet areas, pet policy, to a free in-home estimate and we'll price out a material plan room by room rather than one blanket recommendation.

## How long does it take to replace the floors in a whole house?
URL: https://sarasotaflooringcompany.com/blog/long-take-replace-floors-whole-house/

A two-person crew lays about 1,000 square feet of click LVP in one to two days on a flat, prepped slab. Tile and glue-down wood take longer because of cure times: tile needs 24 hours before grouting and up to 72 hours before heavy loads, and a full hardwood sand-and-refinish runs three to five working days.

### The Baseline: Click LVP on a Ready Slab
A two-person crew typically installs about 1,000 square feet of click-together LVP in one to two days, as long as the slab underneath is already flat and prepped. That's the fastest realistic timeline for a whole-house job, and it's the number most other materials get measured against. The catch is that ready slab. If the existing floor still needs to come out, or the concrete has high spots, add time before the clock on the flooring itself even starts; that's covered by subfloor leveling when it applies. That two-day figure assumes a two-person crew working steadily, not a solo installer squeezing in a job between others. Larger homes sometimes get a three- or four-person crew specifically to keep pace with that same daily rate across more square footage, rather than stretching one crew across a week and a half. We sequence bedrooms and living areas first when the household is staying home during the work, and save less-used spaces like a guest room or den for the tail end of the schedule.

### Why Tile and Glue-Down Wood Take Longer
Tile isn't slow to install so much as slow to finish. Most tile can be grouted about 24 hours after setting, and you should wait at least another 24 hours after grouting before regular foot traffic and 72 hours before heavy loads or appliances go back, according to MAPEI's installation guidance. Rapid-set products can shorten that window. Glue-down hardwood has its own adhesive cure time on top of the actual laying. The grout itself matters too. Standard cement-based grout needs the full cure window MAPEI describes, while some rapid-set formulations are engineered specifically to shorten it, faster turnaround on occupied jobs. Ask which grout is planned for your project if the calendar is tight.

### Sand-and-Refinish Runs on a Different Clock Entirely
A full sand-and-refinish job on existing hardwood typically takes three to five working days. That's the sanding, staining, and finish coats. Oil-based polyurethane needs up to 30 days to fully cure before rugs and furniture pads go back down, even though the floor is walkable well before that. If you're weighing refinishing against a full replacement, our refinishing page covers the tradeoffs in more depth. The sanding stage alone typically eats two of those three to five days, since it usually takes multiple passes with progressively finer grits to get an even surface, especially on a floor that's been refinished before. That's a meaningful chunk of the timeline right there. Staining and the finish coats fill out the remaining days.

### What Actually Slows a Whole-House Job Down
Old flooring removal, furniture moves, multiple rooms with different materials, and custom cuts around cabinetry or stairs all add days that a per-square-foot install rate doesn't capture. A 1,800 square foot home with tile in the wet areas and LVP everywhere else takes longer than either material alone would suggest, simply because the crew is managing two different cure schedules under one roof. Stairs are their own category entirely. A staircase with a dozen or more treads, risers, and stringers to cut and fit precisely can add a full day or more on its own, separate from whatever timeline the rest of the house is on. None of these variables show up in a simple per-square-foot install rate, which is why we walk through the actual floor plan room by room before giving a timeline rather than quoting off square footage alone. That's also why the timeline on your written quote is a range tied to the actual scope, not a single number pulled from a generic rate card.

## How long does it take to refinish hardwood floors?
URL: https://sarasotaflooringcompany.com/blog/long-take-refinish-hardwood-floors/

A full hardwood floor sand-and-refinish takes 3-5 working days from the first sanding pass to the last coat. Oil-based polyurethane needs up to 30 days to fully cure before furniture and rugs go back down, and Sarasota's summer humidity can stretch that further, so we build extra dry time into jobs scheduled June through September.

### How long the actual work takes
Sanding, staining and coating a typical hardwood floor takes 3-5 working days on site. Day one is usually the coarse sanding pass that strips the old finish, followed by progressively finer grits until the wood surface is smooth and even. If you're changing stain color, that adds a day for staining and dry time before the first finish coat goes on. Most jobs get two to three coats of polyurethane, each needing several hours to dry before the next one, which is why the finish stage often takes longer than the sanding itself. A larger home, a staircase in the mix, or rooms with a lot of cut-in edges around cabinets and built-ins can push a job toward the high end of that 3-5 day range. Our refinishing estimates note an expected day count up front, so you can plan around it rather than guessing. Stage Typical time Coarse-to-fine sanding 1-2 days Staining (if changing color) 1 day, plus dry time Finish coats (2-3 coats) 1-2 days Full finish cure before rugs/furniture Up to 30 days (oil-based)

### Why cure time matters more than the days on your calendar
The floor is walkable in socks within about a day of the last coat, but that's not the same as cured. Oil-based polyurethane needs up to 30 days to fully cure before it's ready for furniture, area rugs, and normal foot traffic in shoes. Water-based finishes generally cure faster, which is one reason we walk through finish options with customers who need the room back in use sooner - a rental turnover or a home going on the market can't always wait a full month. Felt pads under furniture legs and a rug pad chosen for hardwood, rather than a rubber-backed one that can trap moisture, both help protect a freshly finished floor once it's back in daily use.

### How Florida humidity changes the timeline
Finish cure time is a chemical reaction, and high ambient humidity slows it down - that's true of polyurethane generally, not something unique to Florida, but our summer humidity runs high enough for long enough that it's worth planning around. We recommend running air conditioning during and after the job to keep indoor humidity in a normal range, which helps the finish cure closer to the manufacturer's stated timeline instead of stretching well past it. A house left closed up with the AC off during a summer trip is one of the more common reasons we see a refinish take longer than the crew originally quoted. This is the same reason we run a slab moisture check as part of our subfloor and prep process before any new hardwood install, not just refinishing jobs.

### Planning your schedule around a refinishing job
Because the space isn't usable for normal living during sanding and isn't ready for rugs and furniture until the finish cures, most customers either stay elsewhere for the work week or refinish one section of the house at a time, closing that area off from pets and foot traffic until the finish is safe to walk on. If you're weighing a full sand-and-refinish against just patching a damaged area, ask us about a partial refinish or repair - it's faster but only makes sense when the color and sheen can be matched to the surrounding floor, and we'll tell you honestly at the walkthrough if a section is too worn for a clean match. Get a schedule built around your move-back-in date with a free estimate .

## How long does a slab need to dry after flooding before new floors go in?
URL: https://sarasotaflooringcompany.com/blog/long-slab-dry-after-flooding-before-new-floors/

There's no universal number of days, despite what general guides claim. A flooded slab is ready when it tests at or below 75% relative humidity (ASTM F2170) or 3 lbs per 1,000 sq ft per 24 hours (ASTM F1869), the same default limits any new slab-on-grade flooring install needs to meet in a Sarasota-area home, whether or not a flood was ever involved.

### There's No Universal Number of Days
A flooded slab dries on its own schedule, driven by how long it sat underwater, how thick the slab is, what type of flooring was on it before, what's underneath it, and how much airflow and dehumidification it gets afterward, not on a fixed calendar date. Guessing a number and installing on that guess is how homeowners end up paying to replace the same room's flooring twice within a couple of years. The only honest answer is that the slab is ready when it tests ready, using the same moisture thresholds any new flooring install requires, whether or not a flood was ever involved, and no amount of experience lets us skip that step honestly.

### The Two Tests That Replace Guesswork
ASTM F2170 relative humidity testing, with probes set carefully at 40% of the slab's total depth, is the current standard most manufacturers now actually require, alongside or instead of the older ASTM F1869 calcium chloride test. The default acceptable reading is 75% RH or 3 lbs per 1,000 sq ft per 24 hours, unless a specific product's manufacturer allows more, the way Shaw's Floorte Pro SPC line permits up to 90% RH or 8 lbs in its own tested system. Here's the full breakdown of how that testing works on a slab that was never flooded; a post-flood slab gets tested the exact same way, just after a longer drying period first and often with more than one round of testing before it clears.

### What Speeds Drying and What Doesn't
Running the AC continuously, adding commercial dehumidifiers, and keeping fans moving air across the slab surface all measurably speed up drying compared to leaving a closed-up, humid room to dry passively. Opening windows in a Florida summer generally does the opposite, since outdoor humidity often exceeds what's already inside. A slab that flooded and then sat closed up for weeks before drying equipment arrived typically needs longer than one where drying started within the EPA's 24-to-48-hour window. None of that changes the target number, only how long it takes to get there, which is exactly why we test rather than promise a date based on how the room looked on day one.

### When We'll Write a Flooring Quote After a Flood
We won't quote new hardwood or vinyl plank on a post-flood slab until it tests within range, because a quote built on a guess isn't a real quote. If the slab is still drying, we'll tell you that honestly rather than scheduling an install date that has to get pushed. If the old flooring is still down, removing it is the first step , well before drying time or a new floor even enters the conversation.

### Why We Won't Give You a Calendar Date Up Front
It would be easier for everyone if we could quote "three weeks" the first time we walk through a flooded home, but that number would be a guess dressed up as an estimate, and guesses are how homeowners end up paying for flooring twice. Two houses hit by the same storm, on the same street, can dry at meaningfully different rates depending on slab thickness, how much of the house flooded, whether the AC kept running, and how quickly drying equipment got started. What we can commit to is a testing schedule: we'll check the slab periodically as it dries, tell you honestly where the numbers stand each time, and only write the flooring quote once a reading actually clears the threshold, not before.

## How long does flooring need to acclimate in Florida before installation?
URL: https://sarasotaflooringcompany.com/blog/long-flooring-acclimate-florida-before-installation/

There's no set number of days. The NWFA judges acclimation by moisture-meter readings, not a calendar, and only starts counting once the HVAC has run at normal living conditions for at least 48 hours. Strip flooring needs to land within 4% moisture content of the subfloor, wide plank within 2%, before installation in a Sarasota-area home.

### There's No Fixed Number of Days
There isn't a set number of days, despite what a lot of general flooring guides suggest. The National Wood Flooring Association judges acclimation by moisture-meter readings, not a calendar. Some jobs are ready in two or three days; a house that just had drywall repaired, or a slab that read borderline on the moisture test, can take two weeks or more before the wood and the subfloor are close enough in moisture content to install. Anyone who quotes a flat "three days and you're good" without measuring anything is skipping the part of the process that actually determines whether your hardwood flooring stays flat.

### What Acclimation Actually Means (It's Not Just Letting Boxes Sit)
Acclimation isn't just stacking boxes of flooring in the room and waiting. It means storing the material, unopened or loosely stacked per the manufacturer's instructions, in the actual room it's going into, under the conditions the floor will live in long-term, while we track how its moisture content changes over time with a meter. A garage that's 15 degrees hotter and far more humid than the living room doesn't count as acclimating flooring for the living room. Neither does a house with the AC off during the week before install, even if the boxes have technically sat on-site for the right number of days. The room has to be living-condition normal, because that's the only environment the reading means anything in.

### The 48-Hour HVAC Rule Comes First
The NWFA's rule of thumb is that the HVAC needs to have run at normal living conditions for at least 48 hours before acclimation even starts counting. That matters on new-construction and post-renovation jobs in our area, where a house might have had the AC cycling on a builder's temporary setting, or off altogether during drywall and paint, right up until closing. We ask when the AC started running at normal settings before we schedule delivery, because starting the acclimation clock too early, while the house is still drying out from construction humidity, gives numbers that look fine on day three and cup by month three.

### How Close the Numbers Need to Match
Once conditions are stable, the target is a moisture-content match between the flooring and the subfloor, not just a low number in isolation. Strip flooring under 3 in. wide needs to land within 4% moisture content of the subfloor; wider plank, 3 in. or more, needs to be within 2%, a tighter tolerance because wider boards show more movement per percentage point of change. We take readings on both the flooring and the subfloor, not just one or the other, before calling a room ready, and we log those numbers so there's a record if a manufacturer's warranty ever needs proof the install followed spec. If the subfloor is a concrete slab, that number starts with the slab test itself.

### Why Vinyl Plank Skips This Step Almost Entirely
Luxury vinyl plank changes the calculus. COREtec's install guide, for example, doesn't require acclimation at all; it calls for installing between 55°F and 85°F with a 1/4 in. expansion gap at the walls. That's one reason vinyl plank is often the faster option when a Sarasota or Venice homeowner needs floors finished between snowbird season and a specific move-in date. Hardwood still rewards the wait; a floor acclimated properly moves less over its first year than one rushed in on a fixed schedule. Acclimation timing is usually the biggest variable in how long a whole-house floor replacement takes , more than the install labor itself.

## Can I live in my house during floor removal and installation?
URL: https://sarasotaflooringcompany.com/blog/live-house-during-floor-removal-installation/

Yes, most Sarasota-area homeowners stay in the house during a floor replacement. A two-person crew clears about 1,000 square feet of click LVP in one to two days, so we work room by room, sealing off finished areas and containing dust, and most families are back to normal in a zone within a day or two.

### How We Phase the Job So You Can Stay
We break the house into zones and work one at a time rather than tearing up every room at once. Since a two-person crew can clear about 1,000 square feet of click LVP in one to two days on a prepped slab, a typical living-room-and-hallway zone is often done in under a day, and you keep using the rest of the house while that happens. Dust barriers go up around the active zone, and furniture gets moved room by room instead of piled up everywhere on day one. A typical Sarasota home has enough distinct living zones, a primary suite, secondary bedrooms, and main living areas, that we can usually keep at least one bathroom and one bedroom fully available at any point during the project. We walk the house with you before the quote to map out that sequence.

### What to Expect With Tile vs. LVP vs. Refinishing
Tile is the one that asks the most patience of you locally, since most tile can be grouted about 24 hours after setting, and needs another 24 hours before foot traffic and 72 hours before appliances or heavy furniture go back, per MAPEI's guidance. LVP is close to walkable right after installation. A hardwood sand-and-refinish is the most disruptive; oil-based finishes need up to 30 days before rugs and furniture pads return, though the floor itself is usable well before that. If your project includes refinishing alongside new flooring elsewhere in the house, we schedule the refinishing work for whichever zone you can most easily avoid for a few days, since it's the step that benefits most from an empty room. Rigid-core LVP splits the difference nicely for anyone who wants to minimize disruption across a multi-room project, since it doesn't carry tile's cure-time wait or refinishing's fume and dust profile. It's one more reason LVP tends to be the default recommendation for households determined to stay put during the work.

### What We Ask of You During the Work
Move small breakables and anything sentimental out of the active zone before we start, and keep pets away from the work area, especially on tile demo days when dust and sharp debris are unavoidable. If anyone in the house is especially sensitive to dust or fumes, we'll talk through which days matter most for them to be elsewhere, particularly demo day and the first refinishing coat. We also recommend having a plan for pets specifically, a crate, a sitter, or a closed-off room farthest from the work zone, since even a calm dog or cat can get anxious around unfamiliar noise and strangers moving through the house for several days in a row.

### When It Makes Sense to Stay Elsewhere
A whole-house refinish with oil-based polyurethane, a multi-material job spanning several rooms at once, or a household with someone especially sensitive to dust are the situations where we'd suggest planning a night or two away rather than pushing through it. For a single room or a straightforward LVP replacement, staying home is rarely a problem. If part of your project involves floor repair from an earlier leak or damage rather than a full replacement, staying home usually isn't a real question either way, since that work is typically contained to one room for a shorter stretch. Ask about your specific situation at a free in-home estimate and we'll map out which rooms need to stay usable throughout the project. We'd rather under-promise on the schedule and walk you through each phase in advance than leave you guessing which day a given room comes back into use.

## Is laminate flooring a bad idea in Florida?
URL: https://sarasotaflooringcompany.com/blog/laminate-flooring-bad-idea-florida/

Not automatically, but it needs the right product and prep: Sarasota's outdoor humidity averages 74% year-round, and standard laminate swells if moisture reaches its core. Water-resistant laminate with a WetProtect-style warranty covers spills, pet accidents and wet mopping, but excludes flooding and standing water. Over concrete, Mohawk requires a 6-mil polyethylene moisture barrier with 8-inch overlapped seams before any laminate goes down.

### Is Laminate Flooring a Bad Idea in Florida Homes?
It's not automatically a bad idea, but Florida's climate takes standard laminate off the table for a lot of rooms. Laminate's core is compressed wood fiber under a printed image layer, and that core swells and delaminates if moisture reaches it, whether from a spill, a slow leak, or humid air working through an unsealed seam. Sarasota's outdoor relative humidity averages about 74% year-round, and while an air-conditioned interior runs lower, a house that sits closed up during a summer trip can drift toward that outdoor number fast. Water-resistant laminate changes the equation somewhat, since it uses a denser core and sealed edges to slow moisture intrusion. It still isn't the same product category as waterproof vinyl plank , and we tell clients that difference plainly rather than let the word "waterproof" on a box do the talking. The confusion between water-resistant and waterproof is genuinely the single most common misunderstanding we run into at the estimate stage for this material. We'd rather spend five minutes clearing that up before you order material than have you find out the hard way after a slow leak sits under a rug for a week.

### What Water-Resistant Laminate Actually Covers
Pergo's WetProtect warranty is a useful example of where the line sits. It covers household spills, pet accidents, and wet mopping, which handles most day-to-day life in a Florida home. It specifically excludes flooding, standing water, leaking pipes and appliance leaks, the exact events a coastal Sarasota county home is more likely to face than a house in a drier climate. That gap is worth reading closely before choosing laminate for a laundry room or a kitchen near an ice maker line, since those are precisely the rooms where a slow, undetected leak is most likely to happen over months rather than minutes. A leak under a dishwasher or an ice maker line can run for weeks before anyone notices a change underfoot, and by then a laminate floor has usually already swollen well beyond what a warranty claim will cover.

### What It Takes to Install Laminate Over a Florida Slab
Mohawk's laminate installation FAQ is specific here: a moisture barrier is required over concrete, and for a floating floor that means 6-mil polyethylene film with seams overlapped 8 inches. Skipping that step is one of the most common ways we see laminate fail early in this market, not because the product was defective, but because vapor coming up through an unprotected slab had nowhere else to go but into the laminate core. We also recommend a moisture test on the slab itself before ordering material, since a barrier alone doesn't compensate for a slab that's testing well outside normal range.

### When We'd Steer You Toward Something Else
We'll still install laminate in a Sarasota or Manatee County living room, bedroom or office with the right barrier in place. We won't recommend it for a bathroom, laundry room, or a screened lanai transition, where water-resistant simply isn't the same guarantee as waterproof. For those rooms, laminate 's water-resistant cousin, vinyl plank, is usually the better call; see our comparison of waterproof laminate vs luxury vinyl plank for the full breakdown, and our laminate flooring cost guide for current pricing on the rooms where it is a good fit. Mixing materials room by room is normal in this market, and we'll lay out exactly where the line falls on your specific floor plan at the estimate.

## How do I keep beach sand from scratching my floors?
URL: https://sarasotaflooringcompany.com/blog/keep-beach-sand-scratching-floors/

Shaw's vinyl care guide recommends cleaning weekly, using mats without latex or rubber backing (which can discolor vinyl), and adding felt protectors under furniture to keep grit from grinding into the finish. A 20-mil wear layer also holds up to sand better than the standard 12-mil grade. For Sarasota-area beach traffic, a weekly vacuum or dry mop before wet-cleaning removes grit before it gets ground in.

### How Do I Keep Beach Sand From Scratching My Floors?
Sand acts like sandpaper the moment it gets walked on, which is exactly what happens at every beach-house entry and pool door from Siesta Key to Anna Maria Island, day after day through the busy season. Shaw's vinyl care guide has a specific fix for the entry-point problem: use mats without latex or rubber backing, since those can actually discolor vinyl over time, and add felt protectors under furniture legs so grit trapped underneath doesn't grind in with every chair scrape. The guide also recommends cleaning weekly with a neutral-pH cleaner rather than letting grit accumulate between deeper cleans. The damage from sand is usually gradual rather than sudden, which is part of why it catches homeowners off guard. A floor can look fine for a year or two of beach season traffic, then show a dulled, slightly hazy patch right inside the main entry once enough fine scratches have accumulated in one area. By the time that haze is visible from across the room, the fine scratching underneath it has usually been building for a season or two already, which is why prevention is so much cheaper than the eventual refinish or replacement.

### Does Wear Layer Thickness Make a Difference?
Yes, and it's worth specifying up front if your house sees regular beach traffic. A 12-mil wear layer is the standard residential grade and holds up fine for an average household, but a 20-mil layer, the usual commercial minimum, resists the fine grinding action of tracked-in sand noticeably longer in a mudroom, entry hall or lanai-to-living-room transition. We spec 20-mil routinely for clients who live near Siesta Key or Lido Key beaches and use those doors daily in season. See our full breakdown in 12 mil vs 20 mil wear layer on vinyl plank if you're weighing that upgrade for the whole house rather than just the entry.

### What About Tile Instead of Vinyl?
Porcelain and ceramic tile handle sand better than any vinyl product, simply because the fired surface is harder than the mineral grit doing the scratching. We don't have a lab hardness comparison to quote you here, but in practice, tile entries in heavy beach-traffic homes show almost no visible wear after years of exactly the kind of abuse that will eventually dull a vinyl finish. If your entryway or mudroom sees sand daily, tile at the door with vinyl in the rooms beyond is a combination we install often, since it puts the toughest material exactly where the abuse concentrates rather than spending that budget across the whole floor plan. A clean transition strip between the two materials at the doorway keeps that split looking intentional rather than like two unrelated projects.

### A Simple Weekly Routine That Actually Works
Vacuum or dry-mop before wet-cleaning, since dragging a wet mop over loose grit just grinds it straight into the finish instead of lifting it safely away. Keep a non-rubber mat at every beach-facing or pool-facing door, swap felt pads onto furniture legs once, and stick to a weekly cleaning schedule rather than waiting until the floor visibly looks dirty or dull to the eye. If your current floor already shows dulling or fine scratches from years of tracked-in sand, our floor repair team can tell you within one visit whether refinishing or full replacement makes more sense for that room, and our cost guide covers typical pricing either way so you know roughly what to expect before we come out.

## Can you install new flooring over existing tile?
URL: https://sarasotaflooringcompany.com/blog/install-new-flooring-over-existing-tile/

Yes, in most cases. Rigid-core flooring can go over existing tile if the tile is fully adhered, clean, and flat within 3/16 inch over 10 feet. If it fails that flatness test or has loose or cracked tiles, removal typically runs $2.50-$4.50 per square foot, more on a thick mortar bed, before the new floor goes down.

### What Has to Be True About Your Existing Tile First
Rigid-core flooring like LVP can generally go over most existing hard surfaces, including tile, as long as it's fully adhered, clean, flat, dry, and structurally sound. Shaw's SPC installation guide sets the flatness bar at 3/16 inch of variance over a 10-foot span, or 1/8 inch over 6 feet. If your tile meets that, skipping removal saves both time and money. This matters most for older Florida homes, where tile was often set in a thick mortar bed rather than today's thin-set method. A mortar bed can still pass the flatness test, but it's worth confirming, since mortar-set tile sits noticeably higher than thin-set tile and can throw off transitions to carpet or hardwood in adjoining rooms. A straightedge and a level are the two tools that answer this question definitively; guessing by eye tends to miss the gradual dips that cause problems months later, once foot traffic and furniture have settled into whatever unevenness was already there.

### When Removal Is the Better Call
Loose or cracked tiles, a floor that fails the flatness check, or a building that restricts added floor height are the situations where removal makes more sense than covering over the problem. Ceramic and porcelain tile removal in Southwest Florida typically runs $2.50-$4.50 per square foot, or $4.00-$6.50-plus on a thick mortar bed, with light thinset grinding adding another $0.75-$1.25 per square foot. Height is the other reason removal sometimes wins even when the tile itself would technically pass. Stacking a new floor over existing tile raises the finished height by roughly the thickness of the new material, which can create a step at a sliding door threshold or leave a range or dishwasher sitting slightly proud of the surrounding floor. We've walked into estimates where a homeowner assumed removal was mandatory simply because the tile was decades old, only to find it passed the flatness check without issue. Age alone doesn't disqualify a tile floor from being covered over; condition and flatness are what actually matter.

### How We Check Before Recommending Either Option
We start with a slab moisture reading and a flatness check using a straightedge across the existing tile, not a guess. If there are high spots but the tile itself is sound, self-leveling can often solve it without full removal. If the tile is failing structurally, we'll walk you through tile removal costs as a separate line item on your written quote before you decide. We also check the transition points specifically, doorways, the edge where tile meets carpet, and any exterior threshold, since those are the spots where an extra layer of flooring is most likely to cause a problem later. If your existing tile has scattered cracks rather than a widespread flatness issue, targeted floor repair can sometimes bring a section back into spec without a full tear-out. That documentation also matters if you ever sell the home, since a buyer's inspector may ask what's under the visible floor. Whichever direction makes sense for your home, the quote breaks removal, leveling, and installation out as separate line items, so you can see exactly what you're paying for at each stage. We'd rather spend the extra few minutes confirming it now than come back mid-installation with a change order. Compare that against our tile installation cost guide if you're weighing a full tile replacement instead of covering the old floor. Either way, you'll know the real condition of what's under your feet before a single box of new material shows up.

## Can you install hardwood flooring directly on a concrete slab?
URL: https://sarasotaflooringcompany.com/blog/install-hardwood-flooring-directly-concrete-slab/

Engineered hardwood can glue directly to a concrete slab that tests at or below 75% relative humidity (ASTM F2170) or 3 lbs per 1,000 sq ft per 24 hours (ASTM F1869). Solid hardwood traditionally needs a built-up plywood subfloor over the slab first, since the NWFA advises against installing solid wood below grade or directly on bare concrete in a Sarasota-area home.

### Engineered Glues Direct, Solid Traditionally Doesn't
The short version: engineered hardwood is manufactured to glue directly to a concrete slab, while solid hardwood traditionally goes over a built-up plywood subfloor first, not straight onto bare concrete. Both still start with the exact same slab moisture test, run the same way regardless of which wood you eventually pick. The NWFA's concrete-subfloor guidance sets the same threshold either way, at or below 75% relative humidity (ASTM F2170) or 3 lbs per 1,000 sq ft per 24 hours (ASTM F1869), unless a rated vapor-retarder system is part of the install. The difference is what happens after that test passes, not whether it's required, and that difference is what actually shows up on your written quote once the numbers are in.

### Why the NWFA Draws This Line for Solid Wood
Solid wood is a single piece of material through its full thickness, which makes it more reactive to whatever moisture is directly underneath it than engineered's cross-layered, more dimensionally stable core. The NWFA's guidance keeps solid strip and plank above grade and off bare concrete for that reason; installers on Houzz describe the same practical rule, that a slab under solid wood traditionally needs a built-up plywood subfloor, while engineered is made to glue direct once the slab passes its moisture test. It isn't that solid wood can't handle Florida, it's that it handles a slab better with a layer of separation.

### What a Plywood Subfloor Adds to the Job
Building up a plywood subfloor over a slab means sleepers or a plywood layer mechanically fastened or glued down first, which raises the finished floor height, adds labor and material cost, and gives solid wood a nailing surface concrete doesn't provide on its own. That's on top of the moisture test itself, and it's part of why solid nail-down hardwood runs $10 to $14 per sq ft installed in our area versus $9 to $19 for engineered depending on width and grade, before accounting for the extra subfloor build-up solid often needs over a slab. We itemize that subfloor work separately on the quote so it's clear what's driving the difference.

### The More Common Path in Sarasota-Area Homes
Most slab-on-grade homes we work in end up with engineered hardwood glued directly to the slab once it passes the moisture test, simply because it skips the plywood build-up and the height change that comes with it. Solid wood still gets specified when a client wants it specifically, or on a second floor over wood framing where the slab question doesn't apply at all. Either way, the moisture reading comes first; here's exactly how we run that test before either product gets quoted.

### What If the Slab Isn't Flat, Not Just Wet
Moisture is only half of what a slab needs to pass before hardwood goes down. A slab that's out of level or has dips from an old pour still needs correcting before engineered can glue flat or before sleepers for solid wood can sit evenly, regardless of how the moisture reading came back. Slab leveling and moisture prep often gets scoped as a single visit alongside the moisture test itself, since both determine what the finished hardwood install actually needs, and both show up as separate, itemized lines on the written quote rather than a lump prep charge that hides what you're paying for. Skipping this step is one of the more common reasons a hardwood floor that started out flat develops squeaks or soft spots within its first year, long before moisture would typically be the cause.

## What indoor humidity should I keep for wood floors in Florida?
URL: https://sarasotaflooringcompany.com/blog/indoor-humidity-keep-wood-floors-florida/

Keep indoor relative humidity between 30% and 50%, per NWFA guidelines, with temperature around 60-80°F, to protect hardwood and engineered floors in Sarasota and Manatee County homes. Outdoor air here averages about 74% RH year-round, climbing to roughly 78% in August, so a well-sized AC system running consistently does most of the work.

### The Target: 30-50% Relative Humidity, Not Just "Run the AC"
The number to aim for is 30% to 50% relative humidity with the temperature somewhere between 60°F and 80°F, according to the National Wood Flooring Association. That's the range where hardwood and engineered wood hold their factory moisture content, seams stay tight, and boards don't cup or gap with the seasons. "Run the AC" gets most Sarasota-area homes close, but it's not automatic: a thermostat set to temperature alone can leave humidity higher than it looks, especially on a mild, damp day when the compressor doesn't run long enough to pull moisture out of the air.
